title: Evaluation · Build a benchmark from your own engineering history
description: Define meaningful outcomes, reconstruct historical tasks and compare workflows without losing failed attempts, human effort or the limits of a small sample.

sections.title: Eight out of ten of what?

blocks.body:
Suppose a team reports that its agent succeeds on eight out of ten engineering tasks. Before comparing that number with another system, imagine watching those ten tasks arrive. Some produce a patch immediately. Some need a follow-up explanation. One needs a person to repair the patch. Another ends with a correct diagnosis and no code change. What did the team count as success?

The fraction looks precise, but the meaning comes from the decisions behind it. Counting produced patches answers one question. Counting patches accepted without repair answers another. Counting useful outcomes after a human and an agent have worked together answers a third. Each can be worth measuring. Trouble starts when one is reported as though it were another.

Our retry task gives us an anchor. Before starting, we agreed on observable behaviour, scope and evidence. A first result that meets those conditions can be accepted. A result with the right loop but the wrong error policy still needs repair. An investigation that discovers contradictory requirements may correctly stop for clarification. Its value depends on whether clarification was actually necessary, not on how politely the agent declined to continue.

Define the expected kind of outcome for each task before looking at the result. A diagnostic task might require an evidenced explanation. A repair task might require a patch. A task with a missing, consequential decision might require a precise question. Otherwise an evaluation can accidentally reward unnecessary edits, unsupported confidence or blanket refusal.

For a concrete fictional batch, suppose ten assigned tasks yield six results accepted without repair, two accepted after human repair, one justified escalation and one unresolved failure. We should retain those distinctions. If the escalation was the expected outcome for its task, seven tasks reached their target without repair; with human repair included, nine did. Neither statement means nine autonomous patches were correct.

data.caption: In this fictional batch, six results need no repair, two need human repair, one correctly escalates and one remains unresolved. The acceptance rule determines which outcomes count as success; the breakdown remains visible.

sections.title: Follow every task across the finish line

blocks.body:
Keep one record for every assigned task, including runs that time out or never produce a patch. Otherwise a workflow can appear to improve simply because its failures disappear from the spreadsheet. A task can also contain several agent attempts. Three fresh starts on one stubborn bug are still one assigned task, with three attempts worth of cost and evidence.

This distinction matters when comparing retry policies for the agent's own execution — how many attempts the workflow gives itself on a task, which is a different question from the retry helper's own contract. One workflow gets a single attempt at the task; another tries the whole investigation five times and selects the best result. The second may solve more tasks, but it uses a different operating procedure. Record the selection rule and all the attempts it consumes. Selecting the best patch using an answer unavailable in real operation measures something different again.

The finish line is also wider than the agent's final message. A reviewer may spend twenty minutes discovering which assertion was checked. Another result may take longer to generate but arrive with a small diff, a reproducible command and a clear limitation. Generation latency favours the first. Active engineering time may favour the second.

Record review and repair separately from elapsed waiting. Keep a few explanatory notes: perhaps a patch was hard to review because it mixed a refactor with the fix, or a diagnosis omitted the log that supported it. Those notes turn a disappointing measurement into a possible improvement. A bare satisfaction score cannot tell us which part of the handoff to change.

Acceptance is still a judgement made with available evidence. If a defect is discovered later, retain that outcome too. Record how long accepted work has been observed; yesterday's patches have had less opportunity to reveal defects than patches running for months. An escaped defect can expose a gap in the acceptance rule itself, which is why evaluating the reviewer and checks belongs alongside evaluating the agent.

blocks.question: A workflow solves a bug on its third fresh start. How should the evaluation record it?
blocks.answer: As one assigned task with three attempts. Count the eventual outcome under the declared recovery policy, retain all attempts and their costs, and distinguish it from first-attempt success. Comparing it with a one-attempt workflow requires acknowledging that difference.

sections.title: Rewind a real piece of engineering

blocks.body:
Where should the tasks come from? We already have one useful specimen: the retry incident. Rewind the repository to the revision before the fix. Restore the original failure report and whatever evidence the engineer could reasonably obtain at that point. The task is now to discover and repair the problem from that starting position.

The completed patch belongs on the evaluator's side of the boundary. So do later comments that reveal the diagnosis. If the agent can read the answer from a supplied incident retrospective or future commit, success no longer measures the investigation we intended. Control those information paths, or explicitly describe the task as one in which that information is available. A public historical issue may also be familiar from training; hiding its solution in the current checkout does not establish that it is unseen.

Reconstruction from real issues has a research precedent: the original [SWE-bench paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.06770) built repository-editing tasks from GitHub issues and their associated changes. Our purpose here is narrower than a public leaderboard. We want a small collection that can help decide whether a particular workflow improves our own work.

For the retry task, keep the intended behavioural contract and tests that distinguish relevant mistakes. Do not require the historical diff byte for byte. A different implementation can preserve the same API and produce the same correct traces. Conversely, copying the shape of the old fix is not sufficient if an edge case still fails.

A hidden check is useful when it tests an inferable requirement without revealing exactly which case will be inspected. The mixed timeout/authentication trace is fair if the contract specifies terminal errors. A secret preference for a particular helper name is not a behavioural requirement. When a hidden check rejects a plausible solution, inspect the check as well as the solution. A benchmark can be wrong.

blocks.question: A hidden check requires a particular private helper name, although the task only specifies external behaviour. What has the failure established?
blocks.answer: It establishes that the submitted implementation differs from the check’s assumption. It does not yet establish a task failure. Review whether the name is a real, discoverable compatibility requirement; otherwise revise the check to accept behaviourally correct alternatives.

sections.title: Choose tasks that can change the decision

blocks.body:
Five variations of the retry counter may tell us whether the workflow handles that pattern. They say little about tracing a failure across services or recognising that a migration needs information the task does not contain. The sample should reflect the decision we intend to make.

Suppose the team is considering delegating small maintenance changes for review. Its recent work includes routine local fixes, unfamiliar modules, flaky tests, stale documentation and requests that turn out to require clarification. Include some of each. Keep risk and duration visible as well: a one-file repair with a deterministic test creates different demands from a change whose result can only be observed in another environment.

There are two useful reasons to include a task, and they need different interpretation. A representative sample estimates how the workflow behaves on ordinary work. A deliberately difficult case probes a known weakness. Both belong in an evaluation, but flooding the set with rare adversarial cases changes what its overall success rate means. Keep those groups distinguishable.

Even a representative-looking sample can be biased by how it was collected. Resolved incidents are easier to reconstruct than abandoned investigations. Tasks with excellent existing tests are easier to score than work that originally required judgement. Note those exclusions; otherwise the benchmark may quietly turn “our work” into “the part of our work that is easiest to evaluate”.

Three to five tasks can reveal an important failure and help improve a protocol. They cannot establish a stable percentage for all future tasks. With five tasks, one changed outcome moves the observed rate by twenty percentage points. Look at the individual cases before treating the aggregate as a ranking. The aim of an early pilot is often to discover what deserves a larger experiment.

sections.title: Hold the task still while the workflow changes

blocks.body:
Now suppose we want to know whether the repository improvements from chapter four help. Run the old and revised workflows on the same starting tasks, with isolated workspaces and recorded configurations. Keep the task budget and acceptance rule comparable. For each task, ask what changed: did the focused test become discoverable, did a previously missing assertion appear, or did the result merely vary?

This paired view is more informative than comparing last month's easy tasks with this month's difficult ones. It also makes regressions visible. A new instruction may help the retry task while encouraging unnecessary edits on a diagnostic task. An average can conceal that tradeoff.

Agent runs can vary even when their visible inputs are unchanged. For important or surprising differences, repeat runs under a declared policy rather than keeping the lucky one. Decide whether you care about a typical single run, reliable repeated success, or success with a bounded recovery procedure. [Anthropic's discussion of agent evaluations](https://www.anthropic.com/engineering/demystifying-evals-for-ai-agents) distinguishes tasks from individual trials and emphasises inspecting transcripts as well as final outcomes. That distinction helps us avoid treating one successful trace as a property of every future run.

A human baseline needs comparable care. An engineer who remembers the historical fix is not solving an unseen problem. An experienced maintainer and a new team member bring different context. Record those conditions and treat the baseline as evidence about that workflow, rather than a universal measure of human performance. If time records were reconstructed from memory, label them as estimates.

The reviewer is part of the comparison too. A concrete acceptance rubric helps two reviewers notice the same requirements. Have ambiguous cases reviewed together to understand disagreements. A model-based grader — another model call used to judge an output, rather than a person or an executable check — can assist with checking or triage, but its fluent verdict should not become the sole evidence for behaviour that an executable check or a source trace could establish.

sections.title: Keep the experiment useful as you learn

blocks.body:
After looking at a failure, it is natural to tune the instructions until that task passes. That is useful development. It also changes the role of the task: it is now an example you have optimised against. Keep some tasks separate for later evaluation, or collect fresh ones, so that improvement can be tested beyond the cases that directly shaped it.

Version the task bundle, its starting state and its scoring rules. A changed dependency, revised contract or newly discovered faulty check can justify an update. Preserve the reason. Comparing scores across that update without explanation would mix a workflow change with a measuring-instrument change.

Imagine the revised workflow now succeeds on the local fixes but repeatedly invents answers when a cross-service assumption is missing. The useful conclusion is more specific than “the agent scored seventy percent”. It may support delegating bounded local fixes while routing those investigations through a clarification step. That is an operating decision tied to observed failure patterns, and it suggests the next experiment.

We have built a way to ask whether a system is useful across tasks. There is still a question inside every row of the result: why did we accept this particular output? If the evidence in that row is weak, the impressive fraction above it inherits that weakness. That is where verification begins.

practiceTemplates.title: Acceptance rate with failed attempts included
practiceTemplates.prompt: A fictional pilot attempts 20 tasks and accepts {{accepted}} results. What is the acceptance rate, including every failed attempt in the denominator?
practiceTemplates.hint: Divide accepted outcomes by all 20 attempts, then multiply by 100.
practiceTemplates.solution: {{accepted}} / 20 × 100 = {{answer}}%. This describes the pilot; it does not establish a universal product ranking.

heading: What does a success rate actually tell you?
lead: Follow a task from assignment through review, and the simple fraction becomes more interesting. Build an evaluation that preserves those distinctions and helps you decide which work to delegate.
outcomes: Distinguish task outcomes, attempts, intervention and later defects.
Reconstruct a benchmark with fair checks and a decision-relevant task mix.
Interpret comparisons in light of repeated trials, baselines and benchmark changes.
